title: Two holding a garment

outline: 2 It teaches one case: I found it and it is all mine
17 Then whose — the rabbis? They say the claimant must prove
19 But for Sumchos, all the more should they divide without an oath
20 Even Sumchos: he spoke of two uncertain claims, not two certain ones
17 Then whose — the rabbis? They say the claimant must prove
19 But for Sumchos, all the more should they divide without an oath
20 Even Sumchos: he spoke of two uncertain claims, not two certain ones
22 Even Sumchos: he spoke where there is a prior monetary link
26 Then the rabbis? They too leave the remainder until Elijah

captions: Mishnah: two hold a garment, each says I found it, each says it is all mine
Why teach both 'I found it' and 'it is all mine'?
It teaches one case: I found it and it is all mine
Then teach only 'I found it'
'Found' alone could mean 'saw'; 'all mine' rules that out
But Rabbanai: 'found' in Scripture means it came to hand
The tanna uses everyday speech, where seeing is called finding
Then teach only 'all mine'
The extra clause teaches that seeing does not acquire
How can it be one case? It says 'this one… and this one' twice
Rav Pappa: the first clause is a find, the second a purchase
And both are needed: a find alone, or a sale alone, would not teach the other
A sale? See whose money the seller took
He took from both, one willingly, one not, and cannot say which
Is the mishnah not Ben Nannas, who forbids oaths that make one side swear falsely?
Even Ben Nannas: here both may have lifted it together, so no false oath is certain
Is the mishnah not Sumchos, who divides doubtful money without an oath?
Then whose — the rabbis? They say the claimant must prove
No: for the rabbis, both holding it is different from neither holding it
But for Sumchos, all the more should they divide without an oath
Even Sumchos: he spoke of two uncertain claims, not two certain ones
But Rabbah bar Rav Huna has Sumchos say it even for certain claims
Even Sumchos: he spoke where there is a prior monetary link
Is it not a fortiori? Here, with no link, all the more divide without an oath
Even Sumchos: this oath is rabbinic, as R. Yoḥanan said, against seizing another's cloak
Is the mishnah not R. Yose, who leaves disputed money until Elijah comes?
Then the rabbis? They too leave the remainder until Elijah
No: for the rabbis, there one coin certainly belongs to one party; here both may own it
But for R. Yose, all the more should it wait for Elijah
Even R. Yose: there a cheat is certain, here perhaps both lifted it
Or: there R. Yose penalises the cheat to make him confess; here there is nothing to confess
That works for a find; what of a sale?
Rather, the first answer is the clear one
For rabbis and R. Yose alike: the shopkeeper's ledger — both swear and collect, though a cheat is certain
There the shopkeeper and the worker each have a claim on the employer alone
And the worker likewise, so both swear and collect from the employer

captions: Mishnah: four primary categories of damage
Since it says primaries, there are derivatives
Are the derivatives like their primaries or not?
For Shabbos: thirty-nine primaries, and derivatives are like them
Then what distinguishes primary from derivative there?
Two primaries together are two liabilities; a primary and its derivative are one
For R. Eliezer, who counts them separately, why call one primary and one derivative?
What was significant in the Tabernacle is called primary
For impurity: primaries defile people and vessels, derivatives only food and drink
And here, in damages?
Rav Pappa: some are like their primaries and some are not
Baraisa: three primaries in the ox — horn, tooth, foot
Whence horn?
'If it gores' — goring is with the horn, as in Zedekiah's iron horns, and 'his firstborn bull… the horns of the wild ox'
Why the second verse?
Lest you say Torah is not derived from the Prophets — the second verse is Torah
Is that a derivation? It merely reveals a meaning
Rather: lest you say the tam/muad distinction applies only to a detached horn
What is a derivative of horn?
Pushing, biting, crouching, kicking
Pushing is written too — why is it a derivative?
That 'pushing' is goring: the verse opens with one and closes with the other
Why 'gore' for a person and 'push' for an animal?
A person has fortune, so the ox must gore; an animal does not
Incidentally: forewarned for people is forewarned for animals, not the reverse
Biting is a derivative of tooth!
No: tooth damages for pleasure, biting does not
Crouching and kicking are derivatives of foot!
No: foot damage is common, these are not
Then Rav Pappa's 'some are not like their primaries' — about which?
If about these horn derivatives — they too intend harm and are your property
Rather horn's derivatives are like horn; Rav Pappa meant tooth and foot
Where are tooth and foot written?
'And he sends' is foot; 'and it consumes' is tooth
The master said 'sends' is foot — without the proof-verse, what else could it be?
Horn is written; tooth is written
Needed: one might have read both verses as tooth
Now that one is foot, whence tooth that does not destroy the principal?
By likeness to foot
The master said 'consumes' is tooth — without the proof-verse, what else?
Horn is written; foot is written
Needed: one might have read both as foot
Now that one is tooth, whence foot that walks of itself?
By likeness to tooth
Let it write only 'sends', which implies both foot and tooth
Without the extra verse one might take either one, not both
They are equal; let both come — which would you exclude?
Needed: one might limit it to the owner sending the animal
What is a derivative of tooth? Rubbing against a wall for pleasure, soiling produce for pleasure
These too damage for pleasure and are your property — so they are like tooth
Rather tooth's derivatives are like tooth; Rav Pappa meant foot's
What is a derivative of foot? Damage with its body, hair, load, bridle, bell while walking
These too are common and your property — so they are like foot
Rather foot's derivatives are like foot; Rav Pappa meant the pit's
What is a derivative of pit? If ten handbreadths is primary and nine derivative — neither is written
'The dead shall be his': ten kills, nine only injures
Still, one is primary for death and the other primary for injury
Rather: his stone, knife or load left in the public way
How so? Abandoned, it is a pit for Rav and Shmuel alike; not abandoned, it is pit or ox
These too are made for damage and your property — so they are like pit
Rather pit's derivatives are like pit; Rav Pappa meant mav'eh's
Which? For Shmuel mav'eh is tooth, already settled; for Rav it is man — what derivatives has man?
Awake primary, asleep derivative? Man is always forewarned, awake or asleep
Rather: his spittle and phlegm
In flight it is his force; at rest it is a pit
Rather mav'eh's derivatives are like mav'eh; Rav Pappa meant fire's
A stone, knife or load on his roof blown down by a common wind — in flight it is fire itself
These too have another force mixed in and are your property — so they are like fire
Rather fire's derivatives are like fire; Rav Pappa meant foot's
Foot? We settled that foot's derivatives are like foot!
Pebbles — half damage, a received law
Why call it a derivative of foot?
To pay from the best property
But Rava asked whether pebbles pay from the body or the best property
For Rava it is a question, for Rav Pappa it is settled
For Rava, why call it a derivative of foot?
To exempt it in the public domain

title: A woman is acquired

outline: 22 Because of intercourse, which Scripture calls a way
22 Because of intercourse, which Scripture calls a way
27 Or: it is R. Shimon, for whom 'the way of a man' is to seek a wife

captions: Mishnah: a woman is acquired in three ways
Why 'acquired' here and 'betroths' in the next chapter?
Because it wants to teach money
And whence money?
'Taking' from 'taking' in Ephron's field
And taking is called acquiring: 'the field Abraham acquired'
Or: 'fields they shall acquire with money'
Then teach 'the man acquires' there too
First the Torah's word, then the rabbis' — she is forbidden to all like consecrated property
Then teach 'the man acquires' here
Because the end clause, 'acquires herself', is about her
Then teach 'the man acquires and releases'
The husband's death releases her, and that is not his doing
Or: 'acquires' might suggest against her will; 'is acquired' means with her consent
Why the feminine 'three'?
Because 'way' is feminine: 'the way they shall walk in it'
But 'seven ways to examine a zav' uses the masculine
'Way' is also found masculine: 'by one way… by seven ways'
Then the verses contradict, and the mishnayos contradict
The verses agree: Torah is feminine, war is a man's
The mishnayos agree: a woman's matter is feminine, a man's examination masculine
Why 'ways' at all? Say 'things' and 'three' in the masculine
Because of intercourse, which Scripture calls a way
That fits intercourse; what of money and document?
Because of intercourse
Two named for the sake of one?
Those too are for the sake of intercourse
Or: it is R. Shimon, for whom 'the way of a man' is to seek a wife
Then the zav's 'seven ways' should say 'things'
There it teaches that the way of overeating brings on the discharge
And 'the citron is like a tree in three ways' should say 'things'
Because the end clause says 'like a vegetable in one way'
The end clause too should say 'thing'
There it teaches the citron's way is a vegetable's way
And the koy's 'ways', and 'one of the ways divorce and manumission agree' — say 'things'
Rather: where there is a dispute it says 'ways', where none, 'things'
Indeed: the end clause has R. Eliezer say 'like a tree in every thing'

title: Written before me, signed before me
captions: Mishnah: one who brings a bill of divorce from abroad must declare it was written and signed before him
Why?
Rabbah: because abroad they are not versed in writing it for her sake
Rava: because witnesses are not available to ratify it
What is the practical difference?
Two bearers; province to province in the Land; within one province abroad
For Rabbah, require two witnesses, as for all testimony
One witness is believed in matters of prohibition
Only where no prohibition is established; here she is an established married woman, a matter of two
Most are versed; the requirement is rabbinic, and they were lenient lest she be stranded
Lenient? It is strict: with one witness the husband can protest and invalidate it
Since it is given before two or three, he checks first and will not undo himself
For Rava, require two witnesses, as for ratifying any document
One witness is believed in matters of prohibition
Only where no prohibition is established; here it is
Ratification itself needs none by right, as Reish Lakish said; the rabbis required it and were lenient here
Lenient? It is strict
Since it is given before two or three, he checks first
Why does Rava not say as Rabbah?
The mishnah does not say 'written for her sake'
And Rabbah?
It should have; but a longer formula would be clipped
Now too he may clip it
One of three is clipped; one of two is not
Why does Rabbah not say as Rava?
Then 'signed before me' alone would do; 'written' shows the requirement is for her sake
And Rava?
It should have; but it would be confused with ordinary ratification by one witness
Rabbah: is it alike? There 'we know', here 'before me'; there a woman is not believed, here she is
Rava: here too 'we know' would be believed, so the confusion stands
For Rabbah, which tanna requires both writing and signing for her sake?

title: From when is the evening Shema recited
captions: Mishnah: from when the priests enter to eat their teruma
On what does the tanna stand, that he asks 'from when'?
And why teach evening first?
He stands on the verse 'when you lie down and when you rise'
Or: from the creation — 'there was evening and there was morning'
Then the later mishnah on blessings should also put evening first
He opened with evening, then treated morning fully before returning
The master said 'when the priests enter' — say 'when the stars come out'
It teaches in passing that priests eat at nightfall and that atonement does not hold them back
As taught: 'the sun sets and he is clean' — sunset holds him back, atonement does not
Whence that 'the sun sets' is sunset and 'clean' is the day? Perhaps it is sunrise and the man is clean
Rabbah bar Rav Shila: then it would say 'and he shall be clean'; 'and it is clean' is the day
In the West they had not heard this and asked it as a question
And resolved it from the baraisa's 'the sign is the stars'
The master said 'when the priests enter' — but a baraisa: from when the poor man enters to eat his bread
Its end clause surely differs; does its first clause?
No: the poor man and the priest are one time
A baraisa: R. Meir, when people enter to eat on Sabbath eves; the sages, when priests may eat teruma, the sign being the stars
Why the second verse?
Lest you say night begins at sunset and they merely worked late
If poor man and priest are one time, and poor man and people are one time, the sages are R. Meir
So the poor man's time and the priest's differ
No: poor man and priest are one; poor man and people are not
One time? A baraisa: R. Eliezer, R. Yehoshua, R. Meir, R. Yehuda, R. Ḥanina, R. Aḥai each give a time
If they were one, R. Ḥanina would be R. Yehoshua
So the poor man's time and the priest's differ — conclude so
Which is later?
The poor man's, else R. Ḥanina would be R. Eliezer
The master said: R. Yehuda replied, priests immerse while it is still day
Did R. Yehuda answer R. Meir well?
R. Meir meant R. Yose's twilight, which is a blink
R. Meir contradicts R. Meir
Two tannaim report R. Meir
R. Eliezer contradicts R. Eliezer
Two tannaim report R. Eliezer; or the mishnah's first clause is not his
'Until the end of the first watch'
What does R. Eliezer hold? Three watches — say four hours; four — say three
Three watches; he teaches there are watches in heaven as on earth
The signs: a donkey brays, dogs howl, a child nurses and a wife talks with her husband
Does he count beginnings or ends? The first beginning and the last end need no sign
He counts the end of the first, the start of the last, and the middle of the middle

title: What is 'or'?

outline: 5 'The morning was light' — so 'or' is day
6 It says 'the morning lit up', not 'the light was morning'
7 'As the light of morning the sun rises' — so 'or' is day
8 It says 'like the light of morning' — the world to come
9 'God called the light day' — so 'or' is day
10 It means: the brightening he called day
11 Then 'the darkness he called night' would be dusk — but until the stars it is day
12 Rather: He summoned the light and charged it with the day's duties
13 'Praise Him, all stars of light' — so 'or' is night
15 Then only shining stars praise? 'Praise Him, all His hosts'
16 It teaches that starlight is light — for one who vows off light
17 'At light the murderer rises… at night he is as a thief' — so 'or' is day
18 There: if it is clear as light he is a murderer; if doubtful as night, a thief
19 'Let it hope for light and have none' — so 'or' is day
21 'Night is light about me' — so 'or' is day
22 There David speaks of this world and the next
23 R. Yehuda: search on the 'or' of the fourteenth and on the fourteenth morning — so 'or' is night. Conclude so
24 R. Eliezer b. Yaakov: from the 'or'; R. Yehuda: from sunrise
25 Their exchange: where is a day part forbidden and part permitted? The day itself proves it, for leaven
26 Since R. Yehuda says sunrise, R. Eliezer's 'or' is night
28 Then R. Eliezer's own night is a part-permitted day
29 He meant: the rabbis divide day from night, not a day within itself
30 Did R. Yehuda's leaven answer hold?
31 R. Eliezer: I speak of rabbinic labour, you answer with Torah leaven
35 A rabbinic fence around Torah law
36 Beacons are lit on the 'or' of the intercalated day — so 'or' is night. Conclude so
37 One who offers all night must wash at 'orah' — so 'or' is night
39 Mar Zutra: miscarrying on the 'or' of the eighty-first — Beis Hillel's reply shows 'or' is night. Conclude so
40 'It might be eaten on the or of the third day' — so 'or' is night. Conclude so
41 On the 'or' of Yom Kippur one prays seven and confesses — so 'or' is night. Conclude so
42 Shmuel's school: on the night of the fourteenth one searches — so 'or' is night

captions: Mishnah: on the 'or' of the fourteenth one searches for leaven by lamplight
What is 'or'?
Rav Huna: daybreak
Rav Yehuda: night
The assumption: daybreak means actual day and night means actual night
'The morning was light' — so 'or' is day
It says 'the morning lit up', not 'the light was morning'
'As the light of morning the sun rises' — so 'or' is day
It says 'like the light of morning' — the world to come
'God called the light day' — so 'or' is day
It means: the brightening he called day
Then 'the darkness he called night' would be dusk — but until the stars it is day
Rather: He summoned the light and charged it with the day's duties
'Praise Him, all stars of light' — so 'or' is night
It means: all shining stars
Then only shining stars praise? 'Praise Him, all His hosts'
It teaches that starlight is light — for one who vows off light
'At light the murderer rises… at night he is as a thief' — so 'or' is day
There: if it is clear as light he is a murderer; if doubtful as night, a thief
'Let it hope for light and have none' — so 'or' is day
There Job curses his fortune
'Night is light about me' — so 'or' is day
There David speaks of this world and the next
R. Yehuda: search on the 'or' of the fourteenth and on the fourteenth morning — so 'or' is night. Conclude so
R. Eliezer b. Yaakov: from the 'or'; R. Yehuda: from sunrise
Their exchange: where is a day part forbidden and part permitted? The day itself proves it, for leaven
Since R. Yehuda says sunrise, R. Eliezer's 'or' is night
No: 'or' is dawn
Then R. Eliezer's own night is a part-permitted day
He meant: the rabbis divide day from night, not a day within itself
Did R. Yehuda's leaven answer hold?
R. Eliezer: I speak of rabbinic labour, you answer with Torah leaven
And R. Yehuda?
The hours are rabbinic
And R. Eliezer?
A rabbinic fence around Torah law
Beacons are lit on the 'or' of the intercalated day — so 'or' is night. Conclude so
One who offers all night must wash at 'orah' — so 'or' is night
'Orah' is different
Mar Zutra: miscarrying on the 'or' of the eighty-first — Beis Hillel's reply shows 'or' is night. Conclude so
'It might be eaten on the or of the third day' — so 'or' is night. Conclude so
On the 'or' of Yom Kippur one prays seven and confesses — so 'or' is night. Conclude so
Shmuel's school: on the night of the fourteenth one searches — so 'or' is night
Rather: both agree 'or' is night; each used his own town's word
Why does our mishnah not say 'night'?
It chose refined speech, as R. Yehoshua b. Levi taught
